parts.title: Songs of stones
parts.article:
Songs of stones

A Vicenza is a pleasant, prosperous city in the Veneto, 60km west of Venice. Its grand families settled and farmed the area from the 16th century. But its principal claim to fame is Andrea Palladio, who is such an influential architect that a neoclassical style is known as Palladian. The city is a permanent exhibition of some of his finest buildings, and as he was born in Padua-to be precise-500 years ago, the International Centre for the Study of Palladio’s Architecture has an excellent excuse for mounting la grande mostra, the big show.

B The exhibition has the special advantage of being held in one of Palladio’s buildings, Palazzo Barbaran da Porto. Its bold façade is a mixture of rustication and decoration set between two rows of elegant columns. On the second floor the pediments are alternately curved or pointed, a Palladian trademark. The harmonious proportions of the atrium at the entrance lead through to a dramatic interior of fine fireplaces and painted ceilings. Palladio’s design is simple, clear and not over-crowded. The show has been organised on the same principles, according to Howard Burns, the architectural historian who co-curated it.

C Palladio’s father was a miller who settled in Vicenza, where the young Andrea was apprenticed to a skilled stonemason. How did a humble miller’s son become a world renowned architect? The answer in the exhibition is that, as a young man, Palladio excelled at carving decorative stonework on columns, doorways and fireplaces. He was plainly intelligent, and lucky enough to come across a rich patron, Gian Giorgio Trissino, a landowner and scholar, who organised his education, taking him to Rome in the 1540s, where he studied the masterpieces of classical Roman and Greek architecture and the work of other influential architects of the time, such as Donato Bramante and Raphael.

D Mr Burns argues that social mobility was also important. Entrepreneurs, prosperous from agriculture in the Veneto, commissioned the promising local architect to design their country villas and their urban mansions. In Venice the aristocracy were anxious to co-opt talented artists, and Palladio was given the chance to design the buildings that have made him famous-the churches of San Giorgio Maggiore and the Redentore, both easy to admire because they can be seen from the city’s historical centre across a stretch of water.

E He tried his hand at bridges-his unbuilt version of the Rialto Bridge was decorated with the large pediment and columns of a temple and, after a fire at the Ducal Palace, he offered an alternative design which bears an uncanny resemblance to the Banqueting House in Whitehall in London. Since it was designed by Inigo Jones, Palladio’s first foreign disciple, this is not as surprising as it sounds.

F Jones, who visited Italy in 1614, bought a trunk full of the master’s architectural drawings; they passed through the hands of the Dukes of Burlington and Devonshire before settling at the Royal Institute of British Architects in 1894. Many are now on display at Palazzo Barbaran. What they show is how Palladio drew on the buildings of ancient Rome as models. The major theme of both his rural and urban building was temple architecture, with a strong pointed pediment supported by columns and approached by wide steps.

G Palladio’s work for rich landowners alienates unreconstructed critics on the Italian left, but among the papers in the show are designs for cheap housing in Venice. In the wider world, Palladio’s reputation has been nurtured by a text he wrote and illustrated, "Quattro Libri dell’Architettura". His influence spread to St Petersburg and to Charlottesville in Virginia, where Thomas Jefferson commissioned a Palladian villa he called Monticello.

H Vicenza’s show contains detailed models of the major buildings and is leavened by portraits of Palladio’s teachers and clients by Titian, Veronese and Tintoretto; the paintings of his Venetian buildings are all by Canaletto, no less. This is an uncompromising exhibition; many of the drawings are small and faint, and there are no sideshows for children, but the impact of harmonious lines and satisfying proportions is to impart in a viewer a feeling of benevolent calm. Palladio is history’s most therapeutic architect.

questions.question: The exhibition is held in a building which has been redecorated lately.

analyses.content: 原文只提到展览在Palladio的一座建筑里举行，完全没有提到这座建筑最近是否被重新装修过（redecorated）。
你可能看到建筑的名字就默认它作为展馆一定被翻新了，但做题时一定要坚持“没提就是没提”，不要自己去脑补合理性。
The exhibition has the special advantage of being held in one of Palladio’s buildings, Palazzo Barbaran da Porto.

questions.question: Palazzo Barbaran da Porto reflects Palladio’s design.

analyses.content: 原文明确指出这座建筑是Palladio设计的建筑之一，并且随后详细描述了这栋建筑里的多个标志性设计特点。
你可能会因为找不到“reflects”这个直接对应的词而犹豫，但“one of Palladio’s buildings”以及后面的设计细节描述，本身就直接证明了它体现了设计师的风格。

The exhibition has the special advantage of being held in one of Palladio’s buildings, Palazzo Barbaran da Porto. Its bold façade is a mixture of rustication and decoration set between two rows of elegant columns. On the second floor the pediments are alternately curved or pointed, a Palladian trademark. The harmonious proportions of the atrium at the entrance lead through to a dramatic interior of fine fireplaces and painted ceilings.

questions.question: Palladio’s father was an architect worker.

analyses.content: 原文清清楚楚写着他的父亲是一个磨坊主（miller），而不是题目里说的建筑工人（architect worker）。
你可能会把后半句他去当石匠学徒（stonemason）的经历错记成他父亲的职业，一定要看清主语到底是谁。
Palladio’s father was a miller who settled in Vicenza, where the young Andrea was apprenticed to a skilled stonemason.

questions.question: Palladio’s family refused to pay his fee of studying architecture.

analyses.content: 原文只提到一位富有的赞助人安排并资助了他的教育，根本没有提及他的家人是否拒绝（refused）为他支付学费。
你可能会因为看到“别人帮他付了钱”，就顺理成章地猜测“他家里人肯定是不愿意付钱”，切记绝对不要用生活逻辑去推理想象原文没提供的信息。

He was plainly intelligent, and lucky enough to come across a rich patron, Gian Giorgio Trissino, a landowner and scholar, who organised his education, taking him to Rome in the 1540s, where he studied the masterpieces of classical Roman and Greek architecture and the work of other influential architects of the time, such as Donato Bramante and Raphael.

questions.question: Palladio’s alternative design for the Ducal Palace is similar to the Banqueting House.

analyses.content: 原文明确提到，他为Ducal Palace提供的备选设计，与伦敦的Banqueting House有着惊人的相似之处（uncanny resemblance）。
你可能会对“uncanny resemblance”这个词组不熟悉从而错过答案，其实它就是题目中“similar to”的同义替换。

He tried his hand at bridges-his unbuilt version of the Rialto Bridge was decorated with the large pediment and columns of a temple and, after a fire at the Ducal Palace, he offered an alternative design which bears an uncanny resemblance to the Banqueting House in Whitehall in London.

questions.question: Palladio’s design is not only for rich people, but also the poor.

analyses.content: 原文提到他不仅为富有的地主（rich landowners）工作，展览的图纸中也包含了他为威尼斯设计的廉价住房（cheap housing，对应the poor）。
你可能只看到了前半句的“rich landowners”就急着选False，做题一定要把整句话看完，转折词“but”后面的往往才是关键。
Palladio’s work for rich landowners alienates unreconstructed critics on the Italian left, but among the papers in the show are designs for cheap housing in Venice.

questions.question: The show includes paintings done by famous artists.

analyses.content: 原文提到展览中包含了由Titian、Canaletto等著名艺术家创作的肖像画和风景画。
你可能因为不认识这些外国艺术家的名字而不敢选，但请记住，在英文里，大写名字并列出现时，通常就是在举例说明题目里的“famous artists”。

Vicenza’s show contains detailed models of the major buildings and is leavened by portraits of Palladio’s teachers and clients by Titian, Veronese and Tintoretto; the paintings of his Venetian buildings are all by Canaletto, no less.

groups.description:
Do the following statements agree with the information given in Reading Passage 1?
In boxes 1–7 on your answer sheet, write:

groups.contentHtml:
8 What did Palladio do in Vicenza before he became an architect?
9 Who covered the fee of Palladio’s architectural studies?
10 Who was the first non-domestic student influenced by Palladio?
11 What kind of ancient Roman buildings affected Palladio’s work deeply?
12 What text strengthened Palladio’s reputation?
13 According to the writer’s opinion, what will visitors feel about the exhibition?

analyses.content: 原文说他作为一个年轻人时（即成为建筑师之前），非常擅长雕刻装饰性石刻（carving decorative stonework）。
你可能会往回看到第10句的“apprenticed to a skilled stonemason”就想写stonemason，但题目问的是他“做”了什么动作（What did Palladio do），而不是他的身份。

How did a humble miller’s son become a world renowned architect? The answer in the exhibition is that, as a young man, Palladio excelled at carving decorative stonework on columns, doorways and fireplaces.
原文清晰写出是一位名叫Gian Giorgio Trissino的富有赞助人安排并负责了他的教育。
你可能会把后面的“landowner and scholar”当成答案填上去，但题目问的是“Who（谁）”，应该优先填最直接的人名。

He was plainly intelligent, and lucky enough to come across a rich patron, Gian Giorgio Trissino, a landowner and scholar, who organised his education, taking him to Rome in the 1540s, where he studied the masterpieces of classical Roman and Greek architecture and the work of other influential architects of the time, such as Donato Bramante and Raphael.
原文中的“first foreign disciple（第一个外国门徒）”完美对应了题目里的“first non-domestic student”，这个人就是Inigo Jones。
你可能会对“disciple（门徒）”这个词不熟，但只要依靠“first foreign”去定位，你也能精准锁定它前面跟着的人名。
Since it was designed by Inigo Jones, Palladio’s first foreign disciple, this is not as surprising as it sounds.
原文说他借鉴古罗马建筑，并在下一句直接点出他乡村和城市建筑的主要主题是寺庙建筑（temple architecture）。
你可能只看到上一句的“buildings of ancient Rome”就卡住了，记住一定要往后接着读才能找到具体受影响最深的建筑类型。

What they show is how Palladio drew on the buildings of ancient Rome as models. The major theme of both his rural and urban building was temple architecture, with a strong pointed pediment supported by columns and approached by wide steps.
原文直接对应说他的名声（reputation）被他所写的一本书（text）滋养壮大，书名就是Quattro Libri dell’Architettura。
你可能会觉得这个意大利语书名太长或者太奇怪而不敢抄，但在寻找书本、文本类答案时，只要它是带着双引号、紧跟着text后面的专有名词，放心照抄就对了。
In the wider world, Palladio’s reputation has been nurtured by a text he wrote and illustrated, "Quattro Libri dell’Architettura".
原文在最后总结时写道，展览的元素传递给观众（viewer对应visitors）一种感觉（feeling），即善意的平静（benevolent calm）。
你可能会在前半句的一堆细节里迷失，一定要抓住题目里的核心动作“feel”，直接去原文找跟情绪或感受直接挂钩的词汇。

This is an uncompromising exhibition; many of the drawings are small and faint, and there are no sideshows for children, but the impact of harmonious lines and satisfying proportions is to impart in a viewer a feeling of benevolent calm.
